<reason>PRO built the debate around one physical claim (lead time is the only scarce resource) and then used the exchange to strip CON's position down to it. By Rebuttal 1 PRO had shown CON already wants permanent surveys; by the pressure round PRO extracted that CON also wants a ready DART design, bookable lift, and negotiated protocols. CON's "eyes, not a loaded gun" distinction is real, but it leaves CON defending something much closer to the motion than a "research niche." PRO's Q2 forced CON to commit to a concrete seven-year timeline, and PRO's closing landed the sharpest unanswered blow: CON's schedule depends on "crash funding when a city is named," yet at discovery no city is named, so the funding trigger arrives late and the plan manufactures the corridor-shifting fight CON itself fears. CON did real damage too—the "one bus is both striker and tractor" critique was a fair engineering hit, the scout-must-fly-first point in the closing was clever, and "readiness buys upkeep bills, not lead time" was memorable—but CON never addressed the funding-trigger problem and asserted rather than showed that characterization eats years even with a standing scout. PRO's two clipped turns are an execution cost that narrows the margin, but PRO made the decisive clash easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing [A5.3–A5.5] turning CON's own seven-year timeline [B4.2] against it: every year spoken for, resting on crash funding that cannot start at year one because the impact corridor is still a probability smear—while the concessions needed to make even that schedule work already amount to the motion minus the parked bus.</best_rebuttal>
